'''''Bromus arvensis''''', the '''field brome''', is a [[brome grass]] native to [[Europe]] and [[Asia]]. The [[Botanical name#Components of plant names|specific epithet]] ''arvensis'' is [[Latin]], meaning "of cultivated land".

==Description==

''Bromus arvensis'' is an [[annual plant|annual]] or [[biennial plant|biennial]] grass with erect [[Culm (botany)|culms]] growing {{convert|0.3-0.9|m|abbr=on}} tall. The grass has an extensive fibrous root system. The leaf sheaths are softly pubescent and leaf blades are pubescent on both faces. The leaf blades are {{convert|10-20|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2-6|mm|abbr=on}} wide. The obtuse [[ligule]]s are {{convert|1-1.5|mm|abbr=on}} long. The large, open panicles are {{convert|10-30|m|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|4-20|cm|abbr=on}} wide, with ascending branches that droop at their ends. The straight or slightly curved branches are typically longer than the [[spikelet]]s. The [[lanceolate]] spikelets are {{convert|1.5-3|cm|abbr=on}} long and become purplish at maturity. The spikelets have long [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s and are five to twelve flowered. The bases of [[floret]]s can be concealed or obvious at maturity. The [[glume]]s are glabrous. The lower glumes are three-veined and {{convert|4-6|mm|abbr=on}} long, and the upper glumes are five-veined and {{convert|5-8|mm|abbr=on}} long. The obtuse and glabrous or slightly scabrous [[Lemma (botany)|lemma]]s are {{convert|7-8|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1.1-1.5|mm|abbr=on}} wide, and have seven faint nerves. The margins are translucent and end in lengthy and acute teeth. The [[Awn (botany)|awn]]s are straight and {{convert|7-10|mm|abbr=on}} long. The [[anther]]s are approximately {{convert|4|mm|abbr=on}} long. The [[caryopsis|caryopses]] are shorter than the [[Palea (botany)|palea]]s and can be either weakly or strongly rolled inwards.<ref name=Manual>{{cite book |title=Gray's Manual of Botany |author= Merrit Lyndon Fernald |year= 1970 |editor= R. C. Rollins |publisher= D. Van Nostrand Company |edition= Eighth (Centennial) - Illustrated|isbn= 0-442-22250-5 |page= 102}}</ref><ref name=Flora>{{cite book |title= Flora of North America: North of Mexico |volume= 24 |author= Flora of North America Editorial Committee |publisher= Oxford University Press |year= 1993 |isbn= 9780195310719 |page= 228}}</ref>

The grass flowers in June and July.

==Habitat and distribution==

''Bromus arvensis'' grows along roadsides, in disturbed areas, and in fields. It is native to southern and central [[Europe]], but is now naturalized as a weed throughout temperate regions including North America and Asia. The grass is a soil improver and is useful for [[erosion]] control.<ref name=Flora/><ref>{{cite book |title= CRC World Dictionary of Grasses: Common Names, Scientific Names, Eponyms, Synonyms, and Etymology |author= Umberto Quattrocchi |publisher= CRC Press |year= 2006 |isbn= 9781420003222 |page= 364}}</ref>
